title: Canada Warns International Students on Work Rules After Indian Permit Rejections
excerpt: IRCC issued a clarification on off-campus work limits after more than 1,500 Indian students at a Calgary college had post-graduation work permits refused.
body:
• IRCC reminded international students they can only work up to 24 hours per week off campus while classes are in session, warning that violations carry serious consequences.
  • The clarification followed mass post-graduation work permit (PGWP) rejections affecting more than 1,500 students — mostly Indian — at Portage College in Calgary.
  • Students who paid over $32,000 in tuition for a two-year business management diploma say they were told their programs no longer qualify for work permits.
  • Portage College has scheduled meetings with affected students and urged them to retain all immigration documents while seeking legal advice.

IRCC Restates Off-Campus Work Limits

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) has issued a pointed reminder to international students about the rules governing employment while studying, following a wave of post-graduation work permit refusals that has left hundreds of Indian students in Calgary without legal authorization to work.

https://x.com/junonewscom/status/2081175896292307214

In a statement posted on X, the agency stressed three conditions: students may only work in Canada if their study permit explicitly allows it, off-campus work is capped at 24 hours per week during academic sessions, and exceeding that limit constitutes a study permit violation with consequences ranging from inadmissibility findings to removal from Canada.

"Working more than you are allowed is a violation of your study permit conditions, which can have serious consequences."

— IRCC, statement on X

The timing of the statement was deliberate. It arrived days after Indian students at Portage College in Calgary staged protests over rejected work permits, drawing national media coverage and raising questions about institutional accountability in Canada's international education sector.

The Portage College Crisis

More than 1,500 international students — the vast majority of them Indian nationals — enrolled in a business management diploma program offered jointly by Portage College and the Canadian Institute of Osteopathic Therapy in Calgary now find themselves in legal limbo. After completing two-year programs costing upward of $32,000 in tuition alone, these graduates discovered their applications for post-graduation work permits had been refused.

The students claim that IRCC changed its eligibility criteria, rendering non-credit programs ineligible for PGWPs. IRCC has denied making any rule changes, pointing out that some graduates from the same institution successfully obtained permits. The contradiction has fueled frustration among those left without work authorization.

"My father spent his whole lifetime saving for me. After completing my two years of study, I thought I would be able to work and gain some Canadian experience."

— Jaspinder Kaur, affected student, to CTV News

Calgary immigration lawyer Laura-Anne Goulding of Shory Law told CTV News that her office alone is handling 200 cases from the college. Mukul Rana, another affected student, called the situation "a betrayal of thousands of international students" and described it as "not just administrative" but "a human crisis."

College Responds, Urges Document Retention

Portage College posted an update on its website on July 21 acknowledging the issue and stating it "continues to seek clarification regarding this issue." The college has scheduled a follow-up meeting with representatives from the affected student group.

In the meantime, it advised students to retain copies of all immigration-related documents, including study permits, letters of acceptance, enrollment records, transcripts, PGWP applications, IRCC refusal letters, and any correspondence with authorized immigration representatives. The college urged those affected to seek professional legal advice.

Broader Context for Indian Students in Canada

Indian nationals have historically made up close to 40 percent of Canada's international student population, making them disproportionately affected by shifts in immigration policy. The Portage College situation comes amid a broader tightening of student immigration rules. Canada reinstated the 24-hour weekly cap on off-campus work after temporarily lifting it during the pandemic, and has imposed stricter requirements on post-graduation work permit eligibility.

In a separate policy change effective April 1, 2026, IRCC eliminated the requirement for a separate co-op work permit for post-secondary students in mandatory placements. While that reform simplified administrative processes, the Portage College rejections have underscored ongoing confusion about which programs and institutions actually qualify graduates for the work permits many consider essential to their immigration pathway.

What Comes Next

The affected students face a narrowing window. PGWP re-applications must be submitted within 180 days of program completion. Those whose permits were refused may need to explore reconsideration requests, federal court judicial reviews, or alternative immigration pathways.

Portage College's scheduled meeting with student representatives could provide clarity on whether the institution plans to take collective action or assist with appeals. For the broader international student community, IRCC's statement served as an unmistakable warning: work authorization rules will be strictly enforced, and violations — even minor ones — can derail an immigration case entirely.
nri_angle: Thousands of Indian students in Calgary face work permit refusals after completing expensive diploma programs, with IRCC tightening enforcement of work authorization rules.
